A couple of interesting posts in @C_Barraud's packed Thursday Brief indicate that while China’s stock rescue package got a shrug, as I posted on Tuesday, the US midterm results got a rally.

After Beijing rolled out its 2024-style support tools on Monday, the CSI 300 slipped 0.2% Tuesday and the tech-heavy Star 50 fell 3.8%. Then Democrats swept both chambers of Congress, and the CSI 300 jumped 2.3% Wednesday, its best day since July. It added 0.3% Thursday to 4,113, up 2.6% in two sessions.

Hong Kong followed with a bigger move Thursday:
▪️ The Hang Seng rose 3.7%, its best day since February 2025 (+4.0% on February 21, 2025, during the DeepSeek rally). It’s now up about 8% from its October 22 low.
▪️ The Hang Seng Tech rose 5.6%, the most since February 2025, per Bloomberg.
▪️ Alibaba and Tencent each rose more than 7%, and Meituan added 6.8%.

Investors are reading the result as a risk to the US AI hardware trade and rotating into value. China’s internet platforms are about as cheap as large-cap tech gets: Bloomberg notes the Hang Seng Tech traded at 13 times forward earnings last month, the lowest since 2024. Bloomberg Intelligence’s Marvin Chen sees three rotations at once. Money is moving out of Korea and Taiwan into China, into value after China was “stuck at trough valuations” while the rest of the world rallied, and away from “tech hardware and pure AI plays.”

The same rotation shows up in the US. Bespoke says 91.5% of consumer discretionary stocks are above their 50-day averages, the highest in at least a year, compared with 35.5% of tech stocks.

Positioning added fuel. Short selling was 32% of Hong Kong’s turnover on Tuesday, the highest in more than three years, according to Bloomberg. Lotus Asset Management’s Hao Hong calls the move “one of the biggest short squeezes in recent years.” The cost of hedging the Hang Seng Tech fell to its lowest since July, and options volume on the Tracker Fund hit a one-year high as bullish bets dominated.

To be fair to Beijing, Bloomberg also reported stepped-up national-team buying and buybacks Wednesday, so the policy floor is perhaps part of this. 

A caveat: Big up days aren’t reliable bottoms. Since 2000, the Hang Seng has had 53 separate days of 3.5% or more. While a month later it was higher 62% of the time (median +3.0%), three months later it was a coin flip: higher 53% of the time, with a median gain of 1.5%.

October brought a significant reset across Technology and the AI complex, but remarkably little broad-based selling… with investors rotating into other parts of the market rather than indiscriminately reducing equity exposure.

The underlying demand picture has also changed. Retail has bought US equities for 22 consecutive sessions (the sixth longest and fifth largest buying streak since 2017 - chart), corporate buyback windows are reopening, and CTA positioning has fallen to -3.3 standard deviations, leaving considerable room for systematic buying as markets recover. 

Meanwhile, earnings continue to beat elevated expectations, while valuations across semiconductors and AI infrastructure have compressed sharply.

We believe the combination of light positioning, returning corporate demand, persistent retail buying, and historically favorable post-midterm seasonality creates a compelling setup for US equities into year-end. With the election behind us and volatility potentially normalizing, there is considerable capacity for investors to rebuild risk.

Bloomberg Economics has built a new inflation gauge, the Bloomberg Price Project, from millions of prices (web scrapes, card transactions, pharmacy data).

Its take: inflation is too high, but the drivers are narrow (oil and AI), which argues against urgent Fed hikes. Anna Wong, Bloomberg’s chief US economist and the lead author, expects the Fed to stay on hold through year-end.

▪️ Bloomberg Price Project headline 4.4% in September vs CPI 3.7%
▪️ But its trimmed mean (outliers cut across 30,000+ products) is 2.2% through October, vs the Cleveland Fed’s 2.7% and the Dallas Fed’s trimmed mean PCE at 2.3%
▪️ Rising: motor fuel +39.9% y/y, airfares +31.3%, software and memory +28.2%, laptops +57%
▪️ Falling: prescription drugs −7.3%, car insurance −5.5%
▪️ Groceries +2.9%, housing +3.1%; tariffs a one-time jump, not lasting inflation

Its key chart sorts every goods product into buckets by how fast its price is rising (below 0%, 0% to 5%, 5% to 10% and so on), weighted by how much households spend on each: 68% of goods spending saw price changes of 0% to 5% so far this year, vs 27% in 2022.

I ran the same exercise (12-month price changes weighted by share of spending) on BEA’s detailed PCE data (211 categories, goods and services):
▪️ The hot tail is narrow: 16% of spending is rising more than 5% y/y vs 60% in September 2022 (11% average 2000–2019). The biggest pieces are gasoline, airfares, software and portfolio management fees. Oil, AI and stocks.
▪️ But the middle is stuck: 43% of spending is rising 3% to 5% vs a 25% norm, led by owners’ housing, hospitals and restaurants
▪️ 59% of spending is rising faster than 3% vs a 35% pre-pandemic average (55% vs 33% excluding housing)
▪️ That middle was just as wide a year ago (42.5% in September 2025), before gasoline took off

So the data agree that the extremes are oil and AI. But that doesn’t explain a 3%–5% middle that has been there for a year, and that middle is why core PCE is still 3.12% and the hawks are hawkish. 

October CPI is November 10. Watch shelter and core services.

It was driven mostly by a -0.17% pullback in the contribution from consumption (to +1.77% from +1.94%), with smaller declines in inventories (-0.05%), net exports (-0.04%) and residential investment (-0.03%).

As a reminder, the Atlanta Fed’s tracker started very strong in each of Q1, Q2 and Q3 before falling sharply as we approached the actual GDP reads: Q1 went from 3.13% to 1.99%, Q2 from 3.70% to 1.50%, and Q3 from 4.95% to 3.37%.

The reading for now remains well above the blue chip consensus* of ~+2.1%.

Here’s the breakdown of the components as of November 4th and changes from my last update November 2nd:

Consumption = +1.77% (-0.17%)

Nonresidential fixed investment (biz spending) = +1.34% (-0.02%)

Inventories = +0.55% (-0.05%)

Gov’t = +0.21% (0.00%)

Residential investment = +0.02% (-0.03%)

Net exports = -0.46% (-0.04%)

GDPNow Forecast: +3.44% (-0.30%)

ISM’s October services PMI eased 0.4 point to 54.5 (est 54.8), a 28th straight month of expansion. For the first time since February, all 10 of ISM’s services indexes were in expansion for only the 2nd time since March 2021 

The 12-month average rose for a 10th straight month. 15 of 18 industries expanded.

▪️ Business activity though −2.7 to 53.8, the lowest since September 2025
▪️ New orders −3.9 to 55.9, a 17th month of growth, with just Construction seeing falling orders (for a third month)
▪️ Employment +1.3 to 51.4, the highest since February and a second month of expansion
▪️ Backlogs +1.4 to 58.0, the highest since July 2022
▪️ Supplier deliveries +3.5 to 56.7, the highest (slowest deliveries) since April
▪️ Prices paid −1.0 to 73.0, above 70 in seven of the past eight months, with the 12-month average the highest since April 2023; again this month no industry reported paying lower prices

ISM’s Steve Miller said many respondents haven’t yet passed higher fuel and tariff costs on to customers, which “indicates that more pricing pressure is on the way.”
